title: De Zerbi Praises Maddison, Kulusevski and Reveals Shocking Truth About New Tottenham Injuries
body:
Tottenham Hotspur finally broke their Premier League drought on Monday, edging Coventry City 3‑1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and giving Roberto De Zerbi his first win in charge after 536 days without a league triumph. The victory sparked a marathon press conference in which the Italian manager unpacked the performances of James Maddison, Dejan Kulusevski and the club’s injury list, offering a surprisingly candid assessment of the squad’s progress and the challenges that lie ahead.

De Zerbi opened by praising Maddison’s influence, noting that the England midfielder’s “vision and timing” had been pivotal in unlocking Coventry’s defence. “James is the engine that drives us forward,” the manager said, highlighting the midfielder’s 71‑minute spell in which he linked play, created two clear‑cut chances and scored the opening goal. De Zerbi added that Maddison’s work rate off the ball has improved dramatically since his arrival, and that the coaching staff have been focusing on refining his decision‑making in the final third to make him a more consistent threat. “When he is in rhythm, he can dictate the tempo of the whole team,” he observed, suggesting that the English playmaker could become the fulcrum of Tottenham’s attacking identity if he maintains his current form.

The spotlight then shifted to Dejan Kulusevski, whose impact has been a subject of intense debate among fans and pundits alike. De Zerbi defended the Swedish winger’s recent performances, emphasizing his versatility and willingness to adapt to different roles. “Kulusevski is a player who can operate on either flank, cut inside or stretch the defence,” the manager explained. He pointed to the winger’s contribution in the second half, where Kulusevski’s pace and intelligent movement created space for the likes of Son Heung‑min and Lucas Moura, culminating in a decisive assist for the winning goal. While acknowledging that Kulusevski has yet to hit a consistent scoring rhythm, De Zerbi stressed that the player’s “work ethic and tactical intelligence” are exactly what the squad needs to navigate a congested fixture list.

Injury concerns, however, remain a persistent thorn in Tottenham’s side. De Zerbi addressed the latest setbacks – a hamstring strain to Harry Kane and a lingering ankle issue for Cristian Romero – with a measured tone. He admitted that the timing of these injuries was “unfortunate” but insisted that the depth of the squad would allow the team to cope. “We have players stepping up in training, and the medical department is doing everything possible to get them back quickly and safely,” he said, refusing to speculate on exact return dates. When pressed about the club’s broader injury crisis, the manager revealed a “surprising answer”: the club has been deliberately rotating younger players to manage workload, a strategy that has inadvertently exposed the senior group to higher risk but also accelerated the development of the next‑generation talent.

Beyond the immediate tactical analysis, De Zerbi used the platform to outline a longer‑term vision for Tottenham. He highlighted the importance of building a cohesive unit that can sustain pressure over a 38‑game season, rather than relying on sporadic bursts of brilliance. The manager underscored the club’s investment in sports science and data analytics, which he believes will help mitigate future injury spikes and optimise player performance. “We are moving towards a model where every decision – from training intensity to matchday rotations – is informed by evidence,” he asserted, signalling a shift away from the reactionary management style that has plagued the team in recent years.

Looking ahead, De Zerbi’s optimism is tempered by realism. The next fixtures pit Tottenham against a high‑flying Liverpool side and a resilient Brentford outfit, both of which will test the squad’s defensive solidity and attacking fluidity. The manager concluded by urging patience from supporters, reminding them that “building a winning culture takes time, but the foundations are now in place.” If the blend of tactical clarity, player development and injury management he described can be sustained, Tottenham may finally translate this long‑awaited win into a consistent run of results, ending a season that has, until now, been defined by frustration and missed opportunities.
